article.title: Serbian prosecutor who investigated Belgrade Trump tower project ‘targeted with spyware’
article.full_text: A Serbian prosecutor who investigated the authorities’ allegedly illegal scheme to help the Trumps build a tower in Belgrade has been targeted with advanced spyware, expert analysis indicates. The finding suggests a disturbing new element in the authoritarian Serbian regime’s campaign to undermine what is believed to be the first criminal case related to global moneymaking drive of the US president’s family, which critics describe as a “pay to play” scheme trading the Trump administration’s favour for business opportunities. Rade Bajić, the targeted prosecutor, said: “In my opinion, my involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack.” Analysts at the Citizen Lab, a digital forensics laboratory, have not so far established who was behind the attack but the Serbian regime has previously been caught using spyware against its opponents. News of the alleged hack follows the Guardian’s revelations last week that Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s president, personally ordered that a cherished site in Belgrade be stripped of its legal protection so it could be handed over for a $500m Trump hotel and tower. Vučić, one of the Balkans’ most influential nationalists, hosted the US president’s son Donald Jr – “dear Don”, as he calls him – and son-in-law Jared Kushner as he ingratiated himself with the Trumps. At the weekend, Vučić responded to the Guardian’s revelations about his role in the scandal by confirming details of a previously secret meeting. He indicated he had done nothing wrong. “I fought for my people,” he said. “And that’s what I’ll continue to do in the future.” Last year prosecutors brought a landmark indictment against senior members of Vučić’s regime, accusing them of abusing their office to unlawfully strip the General Staff building – a monument to Serbia’s recent difficult history – of its protected status. They face years in jail if convicted. Kushner, who was leading the Trump Belgrade development, called off the plans after the charges were made public. Vučić vowed reprisals, denouncing the prosecutors, including Bajić, a member of the specialised organised-crime unit that brought the indictment. Bajić has said he was taken off the case without explanation shortly before the indictment was published. He went on to address one of the rolling protests against the regime triggered by widespread corruption, telling demonstrators in February: “The law will be equal for all.” In August, Bajić received a message from Apple saying it had “detected a targeted mercenary attack against your iPhone”. Citizen Lab researchers, who have been analysing Bajić’s phone, said this was “a high confidence indicator that his device was likely targeted with mercenary spyware, such as Pegasus”. Working with the Share Foundation, a Serbian rights group, they previously identified spyware attacks against anti-government protesters. In at least one case, the Citizen Lab analysts discovered Pegasus on a protester’s phone. “A zero-click infection with Pegasus spyware would not have been visible to the target, and would give the Pegasus attacker total access to the device,” they said of that discovery. The Guardian’s Pegasus Project revealed how journalists, activists, politicians and others have been targeted by governments using the spyware. NSO Group, the Israel-based company that makes Pegasus, has been approached for comment. Vučić, who stepped down late last month and called snap elections for 25 October, hoping to prolong his 12-year rule by switching from president to prime minister. He has been approached for comment, as has the prosecutors’ unit, which has said it may bring more charges in the General Staff building case. Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner have denied they engaged in “pay to play” arrangements and said they were not involved in the Serbian authorities’ decision to strip the building of its protected status.

article.title: Burnham urged to launch inquiry into unequal health impacts of air pollution
article.full_text: The government must hold an inquiry into the unequal impacts of air pollution, 150 scientists, MPs and activists have urged. Research by the Institute for Fiscal Studies shows that across England, lower-income areas have persistently higher levels of air pollution than wealthier areas. The same research found that minority-ethnic populations were exposed to air pollution levels that were about 6% higher than those experienced by white populations. In a letter coordinated by the charity Enact Equality and signed by 150 scientists, MPs and activists, including the climate activist Greta Thunberg, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been urged to hold a national inquiry into the impacts of air pollution on these groups. Exposure to air pollution is linked to heart disease, strokes, cancer, asthma and effects on lung development in children. Despite this, the letter says, the UK does not have a dedicated mechanism to address the health inequalities. Air pollution can come from a wide range of sources, from wood-burning stoves to industrial fossil fuel burning. But the leading threat to clean air is posed by traffic emissions, with petrol and diesel vehicles emitting a variety of toxic pollutants. Measures such as London’s ultra-low emission zone have had a significant impact on improving air quality, with children’s lungs found to have grown bigger and stronger as a result of the policy. While there has been marked progress in reducing air pollution in cities like London, new government data shows that in 2025, parts of London, Glasgow and Bristol still had illegal levels of air pollution. Rosamund Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, the mother of a nine-year-old girl who became the first person in the UK to have air pollution cited on their death certificate, said a “failure of inaction by all the main political parties over so many years, has meant the UK population is exposed to illegal levels of emissions”. This warning comes as new data, obtained through freedom of information requests by the campaign group Mums for Lungs, shows that in 11 English cities and areas, including London, Greater Manchester and Birmingham, more than 200,000 children were taken to hospital with breathing difficulties in 2025. The research found that younger children were the most affected, with more than 120,000 babies and toddlers admitted to A&E or hospital. Children are particularly vulnerable to air pollution because their lungs are still developing and they breathe more air relative to their body size than adults. In the city of Manchester, there has been a stark increase in admissions of babies and toddlers, rising from 653 in 2023 to 1,072 in 2025. Mums for Lungs said the decision in 2023 by Burnham, the then mayor of Greater Manchester, to scrap plans for a clean air zone raised important questions about whether sufficient action was being taken to drive down pollution levels. Jemima Hartshorn, the campaign group’s founder, declared the situation an “air pollution emergency”. “Behind every number is a child who is struggling to breathe and a family looking for help. We cannot keep treating dirty air as inevitable or acceptable,” she said. A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: “Air quality continues to improve over the longer term and while most air quality standards are being met, more action is needed to protect communities. “Our ambitious new targets will cut harmful particle exposure by nearly a third by 2030. Working together with local authorities will keep driving progress through clean air plans and robust monitoring.”

article.title: UK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
article.full_text: RAF Typhoon fighters are to be used in efforts to protect Saudi Arabia from attack by Yemen’s Houthis, flying protective missions over the country’s cities and critical infrastructure as western allies increase their intervention in the escalating conflict. The operation – the most significant military mission signed off by Andy Burnham as prime minister – will involve RAF pilots attempting to shoot down Houthi missiles and drones, which attacked Saudi airports and oil facilities. The Ministry of Defence emphasised that the role of the fighters – whose number was not stated – would be limited. “These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis,” it said. An offensive by the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen that began in September has gradually escalated into a deadly regional conflict. This month the Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia, the backer of Yemen’s officially recognised government. Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid international airport in Riyadh, the deadliest incident since September in a war that has claimed 19 lives in Saudi Arabia so far. Dozens more have been killed in Yemen by the surge in fighting. The death toll from Monday’s Houthi missile strike on a Yemeni government training camp has risen to 73, a brutal demonstration of the rebel group’s military effectiveness. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said in a TV interview the UK had agreed to help Saudi Arabia to counter the “outrageous Houthi escalation that we’ve seen in recent weeks” and said the UK was “responding to protect civilians” from attack. HA Hellyer, a Middle East expert with the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, speculated that the UK could get drawn further into the conflict in the future, asking: “What does defensive mean?” He asked what the RAF would do if a Houthi attack happened on a Saudi ship in the Red Sea and the British were in a position to stop it. “The UK might say it was defensive but the Houthis would see it as offensive,” he said. Streeting, however, said that the fighter jets’ remit was narrow. “RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles,” he said. Military advisers said the UK would also provide an Atlas A400M transport aircraft capable of transporting heavy equipment, in addition to an existing commitment to supply air-to-air refuelling for Saudi fighter jets with an RAF Voyager. The refuelling mission has been extended by 90 days. The UK has long been a military ally of Saudi Arabia: BAE Systems has supplied it with 72 Typhoons in a deal originally worth £4.4bn. Riyadh has been considering buying another 48 in a negotiation that has dragged on for years. Though the UK only had a limited involvement in the US-Israel war against Iran, Typhoons from the RAF airbase in Akrotiri, Cyprus, and in Qatar, flew defensive missions in the spring and summer to shoot down missiles and drones launched by Iran and other proxies against Gulf states. Britain’s announcement came a few days after Streeting visited his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where they discussed how to respond to the Houthi escalation amongst other issues. The US has so far stepped up its intelligence support and sent more than 100 military advisers to help the Saudis with targeting, but it has been cautious about providing more direct military support. Donald Trump urged Riyadh on Friday to accept help from Israel, though it was unclear what was on offer. The White House has been trying to de-escalate against Iran and in the Middle Eastbefore US midterm elections in November and with the oil price over $100 a barrel. The US envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, told a conference in Qatar that sending in ground troops against the Houthis “seems fruitless”.
